vignette:
She is 76, widowed, and still speaks about herself first as a ship captain, as if the title remains the most reliable fact in her life. For decades, she has worked in a world that expects steadiness in storms, quick judgment, and a voice that carries. She is proud of that history, and it has shaped the way she moves through the world now: upright, measured, careful not to show uncertainty. She has lived long enough to know how much can be lost in a single moment, and the event that altered her sense of safety comes back to her with the force of something both sudden and unfinished.

It happens during a confrontation with police while she is much younger, at a time when she believes that if she explains herself clearly enough, the situation will settle. Instead, it escalates. She describes the officers as arriving with a certainty that leaves no room for her words. In the memory she returns to most often, she is not only frightened but deeply disoriented by the speed of it all: the shouting, the hard hands, the sense that she has become an object to be controlled rather than a person to be understood. She remembers the physical force with a precision that still seems to surprise her, as though the body never agreed to file the event away as past. In the years afterward, she can still feel the shock in her chest when she thinks of how quickly authority turned violent.

Afterward, she does what she has always done. She keeps working. She goes back to the routines of command, to the practical tasks that require her attention and keep her moving forward. On deck, she is composed, almost severe, and those around her may not see how much effort that composure requires. She becomes expert at reading faces, scanning exits, watching for signs that someone’s mood might shift. She grows more guarded with authority figures, more likely to anticipate humiliation or punishment even in ordinary exchanges. If a uniformed person raises a voice near her, her body reacts before her mind can catch up. Her shoulders tighten, her stomach drops, and she feels the old helplessness return with startling clarity.

Over time, sleep becomes less restorative. She falls asleep only after checking doors and windows, and even then she wakes quickly, often from dreams in which she is surrounded and cannot make herself heard. In the morning, she sometimes sits at the edge of the bed and tries to orient herself before moving. She says she is not afraid in the way people expect fear to look. She is careful with the word. Instead, she describes a constant readiness, a sense that something bad could happen if she becomes careless for even a moment. This readiness follows her into the present day. She notices it when she is in crowded places, when she hears sharp voices, when someone steps too close without warning. Her body stiffens, and she becomes acutely aware of her age, of how much more vulnerable she feels than she once did.

The years after her husband’s death make the past feel less distant. His absence leaves her with more quiet than she wants. At times, the silence in the house seems to pull the memories forward. She finds herself thinking about the incident while washing dishes, folding clothes, or sitting with a cup of tea. She does not always cry. More often, she goes still. She feels anger, especially at the way the event has followed her for so many years, shaping her trust, her sleep, her sense of bodily safety. Yet she also carries a fierce pride in having continued. She has crossed seas, weathered storms, raised a family, and endured the kind of fear she rarely names aloud.

Now, in the consulting room, she is polite and controlled, but her face changes when she describes the event. Her voice lowers. She pauses before certain details, as if checking whether the memory is safe to touch. She says she has spent years trying to understand how something that lasted so little time could leave such a lasting mark. She is not someone who enjoys dwelling on the past, but she also does not want it minimized. What troubles her most is not only what happened then, but how easily it still enters the present—through a siren, a command, a slammed door, the sudden sight of a uniform. Even now, she lives as though some part of her is waiting for the next moment when power turns against her again.
